subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORISE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES

speechtext:
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) -moved that the House
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

go into committee to consider Bill No. 26, respecting the construction of a Canadian National railway line between Kingsclear and the St. Croix river, in the province of New Brunswick.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Power to construct and complete line described in schedule.

Will the minister be good enough to say if the preliminary survey of this line has been completed? _ He will recall that when the resolution in connection with this bill was first introduced, he stated that the preliminary survey had not been completed, and that was correct at the time. I presume that by this time it has been completed. I merely wanted to know.

No surveys have been
made except a reconnaissance of two alternative distances, rather than routes, one over the 41 miles, contingent upon our being able to secure the running rights, and the other over the shorter course to connect with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Before we go further I might call the attention of the committee to the fact that, as in the case of the other bills, an amendment has been made in section 6 at the instance of the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton).

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Mileage and cost are estimates only but not to be exceeded by more than 15 per cent.

I think it is understood
that we shall include in this and the other sections where necessary the amendments that have been made in the bills which have already passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendments are all included in the reprinted bill.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Issue of securities limited if running rights obtained.

In regard to
running rights, have any negotiations in that direction taken place?

It is not practicable to carry on negotiations for running rights until the company has been given the right to build. When that is done application can be made to the Board of Railway Commissioners for the purpose of obviating duplication.

The government
may exercise that right?

The Canadian National
Railways will exercise the right of appealing to the Board of Railway Commissioners. Personally I have no doubt that some arrangement will be arrived at.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Statement to parliament annually.

I want to be absolutely
fair about this. In a similar section in the other bills I think the committee passed an amendment the other night. The ex-Minister of Finance moved then to add after the word "during" in the first line the words "the first ten days of", together with another slight amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The present section, with the amendments as passed in the other bills, reads:
The minister shall present to parliament during the first ten days of each session held prior to the date mentioned in section 1 of this act a statement showing in detail the nature and extent of the work done, etc.

I suggest that we use the
word "within" rather than during. The latter word almost implies that this presentation is to be made every day. Personally I think the word "within" would be better.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: All the other bills have been amended in this way, and it would seem desirable to have the present bill in conformity with them.

Before this bill is passed, Mr. Chairman, I desire to read to the committee, so that it may appear in Hansard, a resolution passed by the Fredericton Board of Trade at a meeting held on May 14, 1924, in favour of this branch line. The resolution is rather long and enumerates a good many reasons in its support, and in view of its importance I feel I am in duty bound to read1 it. It reads:
Whereas, the Canadian Government Railway system is the important railway system serving the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, with a total mileage of about 2,769 miles,
And whereas, the whole of the province of Prince Edw'ard Island, the greater part of Nova Scotia, and about half of the province of New Brunswick are entirely dependent upon the Canadian National Railway system, both for the transportation of all goods imported, and all merchandises exported, as well as for passenger traffic,
And whereas a very large proportion of the exports of the Maritime provinces go to the New England, and other eastern states.
And whereas, a very large passenger traffic originates on the Canadian National Railway bound for the eastern states,

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
And whereas, the Canadian National Railway system in the Maritime provinces has no direct connection with any American railroad, thus making it necessary for the government system to hand over its freight and passenger traffic for points in the eastern states, to a competitive railway,
And Whereas, this system either increases the freight to be paid on all exports, etc., thereby reducing the returns of the producers, or else reduces the earnings of the Canadian National Railways,
And whereas, there is now before the House of Commons, Ottawa, a bill providing for the building of a connecting link of railway betw'een the Canadian National Railway system in the Maritime provinces and the United States system of railways, from a point at or near Kingsclear, York County, N.B., on the St. John and Quebec Railway, to or near the town of Vancelboro in the State of Maine,
And whereas, this proposed construction is advocated by the directors of the Canadian National Railways as being of great importance in the development of traffic to and from the Maritime provinces and the United States, over the said Canadian National Railways, from a revenue standpoint,
And whereas, a similar policy was advocated by Mr. Gutelius, formerly general manager of the Canadian Government Railways:
Therefore be it resolved, by the Fredericton Board of Trade assembled this 14th day of May, 1924, that it is in the interest of' the patrons of the Canadian National Railways in the Maritime provinces, and in an economic way in the interest of all Canadian taxpayers, that a branch line of the Canadian National Railways be constructed from some suitable point on the Saint John River, to connect with the Maine Central Railway at a point at or near Vanceboro, Maine,
And further resolved, that copies of this resolution be forwarded to Mr. R. B. Hanson, Federal member of York-Sunbury; the Senators from New Brunswick, and the Minister of Railways, the Hon. George P. Graham.
W. J. Osborne,
President Fredericton Board of Trade. Fredericton, N.B., May 17th, 1924.

Section agreed to.
On the Title:

I desire to point out somewhat more in detail what I have already said in connection with this railway. Briefly, the railway is not one which in my opinion can be justified as a matter of business; and I am referring to the subject now only in that respect. In the first place, I would point out that we already have a good many different connections on the Intercolonial with New England points. The next thing I point out is that since this matter first came up we know what the actual freight movements are. On May 5, after this bill had been considered in committee, the following information was given by the minister and will be found at page 1722 of Hansard. He was asked as to the volume of revenue freight traffic transferred to the Canadian Pacific for furtherance to United States points. His answer was:
The tonnage of such traffic handed to Canadian Pacific Railway during 1923 was 187,909 tons and tonnage received during same period front Canadian Pacific Railway was 8,419 tons making a total of 196,328 tons.
Then on the question of receipts he answered :
(a) Canadian National earnings on above traffic were $321,606.65. (b) The St. John & Quebec Railway earnings were $53,255.69 of which the Canadian National retain 60 per cent.
Then with regard to the amount of money which the National system would have earned had this connection been built the answer is:
The Canadian National would have received one hundred per cent of the tonnage shown in reply to Question 1 and additional revenue amounting to $246,917,33.
It will be observed in the first instance, Mr. Chairman, that, based upon actual business- because here we get a photograph of what the situation is-there will be a gross added revenue to the Canadian National of $246,001 odd. I would point out to the committee that another question was answered very shortly afterwards, and it will be found at page 1862 of Hansard. The question here deals with the operating ratios, which give us some slight index as to the amount of money the system would be able to hold out of the $246,000 odd to which I have referred, and it is shown that on the Atlantic region the operating ratio is 123.23; that is, for every $100 worth of revenue received on that part of the system the sum of $123 odd is required to earn it. This added traffic cannot change that ratio very much one way or the other, for those results would be smeared over the whole. Supposing we take this ratio at 120 instead of 123, the result is we would be out of pocket 20 per cent, and, further, we would be out of pocket the whole amount of the carrying charges of the investment. The matter is carried further by the information which my hon. friend gave me yesterday in connection with the operating ratios of this particular line. Hon. gentlemen will remember that we are proposing to build a branch line, from a line owned by the province of New Brunswick, 40 per cent of the receipts from which line have to be paid over to the province of New Brunswick, the Nationals retaining 60 per cent The answers and questions are to be found a page 2264 of Hansard, as follows:
Sir Henry Drayton:
1.	In discharge of the contract to pay 40 per cent of the gross traffic receipts earned on the St. John and Quebec Railways, how much money did the Canadian National system pay the province in respect of the operations of the year 1923?
2.	How much did the said sum so paid fall short of discharging the obligations of the province as the owner of the said railways?
3.	What sum did the 60 per cent retained by the Canadian National Railways amount to in the year 1923?

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

4. By what amount did the said 60 per cent of receipts fail to meet the operating expenses on the St. John and Quebec Railways in the year 1923?
5.	What is the resultant operating ratio of the year's operations based upon the retention of but 60 per cent of the receipts?
Hon. Mr. Graham:
1.	$109,199.75.
2.	No information on this question.
3.	$163,799.64.
4.	$340,455.81.
5.	307.80 per cent.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this whole proposition is absolutely against the interest of the Canadian National Railways. It cannot be defended from a traffic standpoint. These are not my figures; they are the figures of the system. They ought to be an answer to any reasonable man on the question as to the necessity of building this branch. I really think that if my hon. friend is at all well advised he will withdraw the bill. I am quite confident that if parliament is foolish enough to enact this legislation the line will never be built.

Mr. Chairman, while
the information given by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) is correct, I think it should be supplemented by some further information. In the first place, the St. John and Quebec railway, when projected, was to have been built from St. John to Grand Falls to connect with the Transcontinental at that point. Unfortunately only the middle section has been built and it has never been connected with either end. For instance, the last ten miles from Westfield to St. John has never been built and we had to get running rights over the Canadian Pacific into St. John. Three or four years ago I went before our provincial government at the head of a delegation to urge the necessity of completing the northern end of the railway from Centreville to Grand Falls. The then premier informed us that if the Dominion government would build the connecting link, which is the subject of this bill, the province would build the northern end. He said: "Unless this outlet is built we do not feel that it would be prudent for the province to build the northern section and continue to gather freight for the Canadian Pacific." A railway from Centreville to Grand Falls is very badly needed. I venture this prediction, and I have made it repeatedly in this House, that if this connecting link is built, thereby enabling the province to build the northern section, it will be one of the best paying lines in Canada. We simply gather freight to turn over to the Canadian Pacific Railway at four or five different points where we might begin to make something on the haulage of it. We are at

present sustaining a deficit of close to half a million dollars a year on this line, about half of which -is the Dominion's and the other half that of the province. If this completion does not take place we shall continue to lose half a million dollars a year. There is no doubt that the minister will be able to get running rights over the Canadian Pacific from Harvey to Vanceboro. If that is done it will not cost over S800.000 to build the 14 miles from Kings-clear to Harvey, and according to the figures given by my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) himself, our earnings would be increased in the neighbourhood of $200,000 per year. If by spending $800,000 we can increase our earnings by over $200,000, that would be a pretty good showing. If the northern end of this road were completed to Grand Falls it would be one of the best-paying roads in eastern Canada, because all the freight destined for New England states points originating on the whole government system in that country- and there are about 2,200 miles of government railways in the Maritime provinces and eastern Quebec-would be routed over the St. John Valley railway to this outlet, from one end or the other. At present, however, we are simply maintaining sidings, stations, station agents and a train service to gather freight to hand over to the Canadian Pacific at various points. I am sure that the hon. member for West York is candid in his criticism, but if he knew the situation as I know it I am confident that he would revise his remarks with regard to it.

Apparently I
cannot get the interest of the minister, but I will try again. I will take another point: Is it necessary to build lines unless we save mileage? Is it necessary to build lines which largely amount to duplication? Again, is it necessary to build this railway through a territory which twenty-five years hence will probably contain the same number of people that it has to-day? When this matter was discussed before, it was admitted freely that no freight would originate in that territory, that the line would merely serve the purpose of getting freight out. If there is any dispute about that I would sincerely like to hear it. Who is rash enough to say on his responsibility as a member that any new traffic will result from the building of this line in the territory that it runs through? Well, no member is rash enough to make the assertion. Here then, is a place where we get no new traffic. The hon. member (Mr. Caldwell) says it looks to him as if an income of $249,000 would be a good return on the investment. He would be right if we held the money, but the figures brought down by the minister

C.N-R.-Branch Lines
himself-they are not mine-in connection with the operation of the St. John Valley system, show that for every $100 of revenue we pay out in the cost of performing that service $307.80. No one who knows anything about this matter-and I challenge the minister to contradict me if I am wrong-will say on his responsibility as a member of the House that with the construction of this line the operating expense ratio can be cut down to anything like the ratio prevailing on the main line and the system generally-$123 for every $100 earned. Let us know what we are doing; let us understand what our action involves. "We are building a line which cannot pay. This is not a net receipt; it is a gross receipt, and the figures produced by the government show that it costs $307.80 to earn $100 on the St. John Valley line.
Let me go into the matter a little further. In the original discussion the question of traffic over the National Transcontinental as against the Intercolonial was discussed. Nova Scotia business or any other business passing fhrough or originating at Moncton may be routed, first, Intercolonial to St. John and then transferred to the Canadian Pacific. The distance from Moncton to St. John is 90 miles, the distance from St. John to Vance-boro, 91 miles. Hon. gentlemen will observe that Vanceboro is the common point in both schemes. Then again, the traffic may be routed by the Transcontinental to McGivney and thence south over the old Canada Eastern to Fredericton for transfer at Fredericton to the Canadian Pacific. In other words, as matters stand to-day it is open to the management of the Canadian National to route their Nova Scotia traffic, Moncton traffic and that of points further than Moncton, either by the Transcontinental through McGivney or by the Intercolonial through St. John. If the new line is built the mileages will be as follows: Moncton to McGivney, 95.7; McGivney to Fredericton, 34.6; Fredericton to Kingsclear, 16; Kingsclear to Vanceboro, 41; total, 187.3 miles as against 181 at present. In other words, this new gateway which is to be built through a barren territory, producing nothing, is to have a greater mileage than that now available.
Now, as to the north shore and northern New Brunswick business-and I want the minister to interrupt me if I am wrong; we ought to be able to arrive at a common point in respect to a business matter of this kind so that there will be no room either for recrimination or misunderstanding. He has his figures; he knows what his reports are and he will correct me if I am wrong. The north
147i
shore and northern New Brunswick business moves: Intercolonial to Newcastle and Canada Eastern to Fredericton. Potatoes and lumber from Carleton county-and I would like to say something about Carleton county that I know the hon. member representing it will like; It is, I think, probably the best farming county in New Brunswick, it produces a great many potatoes, and Centreville, I suppose, is just about the best point in that whole county-
What about York county?
We come to York county afterwards. The density of farm produce would be very fairly put, I think, at Centreville, and my hon. friend from Carleton will correct me if I am wrong-

You are only getting
into the thick of it there.

I think Centreville is just about the centre. However that may be, it certainly is a very important point. Now their traffic moves on the St. John Valley line to Woodstock, and is there transferred to the Canadian Pacific; the distance there is 25 miles. Supposing, it did not move that way, it would go over the St. John Valley to Woodstock, pass through Woodstock to Kingsclear, 48 miles; you have the total of these two mileages there. But the present business from the north is transferred to the Canadian Pacific at Woodstock. Business now from King's county, which is another very good agricultural county, would run on the St. John Valley from Westfield to Kingsclear, 85 miles. That is what would have to be done if we were going to work it that way. If it went by way of Westfield to Kingsclear it would travel 10 miles on the Canadian Pacific tracks. Now the proposition means these additional mileages, these unnecessary mileages, as against these intervening points of transfer at present.
Here is another point I would put to my hon. friend, and he knows a good deal about railway operation:	Is this line to conduct a
passenger business? Everybody knows it must. My hon. friend I should think at once would say that if the Nationals build this line they are going to put a passenger business on it. Now I wonder if he has ever considered what that means. Everybody knows that the passenger business at this point is passenger business which has to do with the larger New England points. Boston and the like. He also knows that, so far as passenger business is concerned, St. John is the most important point in New Brunswick. Now, just see. how that works out. I have already shown
C.N.R.-Branch Lines



the increased length of haul for freight; let us now take this passenger business, at the points where the passenger business would be heaviest. Se. John would certainly have to have its passenger service; that is the point where .my hon. friend's regular passenger trains on the Nationals are to be found. The passenger haul from Boston and New England points by the new route from Vanceboro, the common point again, would be 140 miles, and by the Canadian Pacific from Vanceboro, 90 miles. What chance is there for anything like a profitable return on a mileage over fifty per cent greater than the Canadian Pacific's movement? I venture to say that my hon. friend has not thought of it. and I think it might be a very good thing for him to think over even now. If the whole object in question is to control cars, instead of handing over traffic to the Canadian Pacific, running rights can easily be obtained on existing mileage, which is shorter than that proposed to be built.
Let us go back for a minute. When this matter was discussed before, the great cry was that the Canadian Pacific held up cars which the Nationals should get. Now, I ask my hon. friend, is there any dispute about that? Is it not true that when this matter was first discussed in this House, and when it was discussed in the committee, the great argument was control of the cars?

One of the arguments,
a minor one.
My hon. friend says it was a minor argument. I do not know that he talked on it. Will the minister say it was a minor one.

My experience with the
shortage of cars last year in the Maritime provinces would convince me that it was an important question. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) gave one or two instances of its importance, from his own knowledge.

Certainly it was a very important question. The information of the House was that the Canadian Pacific were holding up Canadian National cars, and that was the great ground for the building of this line. Well, another question was answered a few days ago, with which my hon. friend is very familiar, and that question was as to how many cars of the National Railways at the end of each month of the current year the Canadian Pacific was holding, and how many cars belonging to the Canadian Pacific the Canadian National was holding, and it was found-the information is on Hansard, and any one can turn it up- (Sir Henry Drayton.]
that in every single month the Nationals had far more Canadian Pacific cars on their tracks than the Canadian Pacific had Nationals on its tracks.

Would you claim this
would apply to the St. John and Quebec railway?
All I am talking about is the figures I am supplied with by the management itself.
That is for the whole National system.

It is the whole system, of course. Railways do not keep separate accounts as to cars over this mileage here and that mileage there; it is the whole system. Of course, it transpired in the committee, and I want my hon. friend again to interrupt me if I am wrong, that there had never been application made by the Nationals to the Railway Board! to compel the return of cars. The whole question of the car business was an excuse, and not a reason; the facts were against it. But let us assume that it was a reason, and not an excuse; let us assume in violence to all the facts that the Canadian Nationals are being robbed of cars. Now, under existing arrangements to-day- and again I am going to ask my hon. friend to correct me if I am wrong-running rights may be obtained over existing connections which would give the Canadian National Railways absolute control of their cars, and would save the expenditure of this large sum of money, with all these resulting railway deficits. Are we interested in keeping down deficits? Do we really want to see something like a proper show given to the National system? Well, we are not going to do it, if in the face of figures produced by the government itself, we persist in throwing away money.
I go back to the alleged reason, and I say that without the expenditure of five cents the system could control its cars. Suppose we stop handing over any freight to the Canadian Pacific at all. Running rights without any new construction can be obtained from Fredericton to Vanceboro over the Canadian Pacific Railway. The minister knows that. He knows that the Board of Railway Commissioners has the power to order running rights.
Under certain conditions.

Does my hon.
friend suggest that under these conditions it cannot be done?

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

They may grant running
rights to save duplication. If there is no duplication threatened I doubt whether they would do so.

I do not know
about that.
It was discussed thoroughly in the committee by counsel for the Canadian National. My hon. friend was there.
My hon. friend has not got the point.
Yes.

No, my hon.
friend has not. The argument advanced by Mr. Ruel as showing the necessity for a pool of some sort was, not that running rights could not be granted unless there was duplication, but that there ought to be a statutory right to operate. But here to-day without the construction of a line, we can get running rights, Fredericton to Fredericton Junction, that is twenty-two miles, and from Fredericton Junction to Harvey, a total of forty-three miles, as against Fredericton to Kingsclear seventeen miles, and Kingsclear to Harvey, a common point, nineteen miles, or a total of thirty-six miles.
No, sixteen miles and fourteen miles respectively, a total of thirty miles.

I got my figures off the map. If they are wrong I want to be put right but I do not think they are much out. It would be a bit longer mileage but you would save an awful lot of money in connection with it, and you would save an operating deficit which is infinitely worse than the whole of the capital expenditure. Now, where does that leave the whole matter? It simply leaves it here:	That on the one hand for
the purpose of getting control of our cars we are to do something that is entirely unnecessary, for, as I have said, we can get these running rights. We are to build this considerable mileage through an absolutely barren bit of country. We are to 'build that in connection with a system the operating ratio of which is 307, so that we are spending, under the company's own figures, $307 for every $100 we get. If this would make such a difference in the St. John Valley system as to make the operating ratio more nearly comparable to the general operating ratio of the whole system there might be something to say for it, but that ratio would be far exceeded here and I am sure the minister knows it. The operating ratio shown for
the whole of that territory is $123 plus for every $100 brought in. That is what is meant here, and I should like the minister to show whether it can be done more cheaply.

My hon. friend has striven hard to get up a good brief against this railway. Two of his propositions for obviating the construction of this line involve in the first place running over the St. John railway, to which my hon. friend objects, and in the second place the Canadian Pacific. These suggestions do not materially help the Canadian National Railway to swell its income. My hon. friend says that if the Canadian National asked for running rights they would be granted. He adds, however, there would have to be some amendment to the act-the railway would have to have statutory power of operation before this was asked for.
I said that was Mr. Ruel's argument.

If that be true, and it was not denied in the committee, unless some agreement is arrived at there can be no running rights unless the Canadian National had operating rights over some other line. In a radway bill of its own the Canadian Pacific Railway Company insisted, as the Canadian National Railway insisted recently, that if a certain line was built by the latter, there should be a clause inserted in the act compelling the Canadian National to make a joint arrangement with the Canadian Pacific. Now, if the Board of Railway Commissioners had the right to order a joint arrangement why the necessity of putting such a provision in the act?
Running rights and joint arrangements are different.

They surely are, but they are a good deal alike. If the Canadian Pacific railway had been sure that it could get running rights it would not have asked for an amendment to be inserted in the statute.
All this talk about running rights
4 p.m. is a bit of a myth unless running rights can be agreed upon between the two roads. The St. John railway does not belong to the Canadian National line. They only operate it under an agreement and its operating ratio of course is high. The Quebec and St. John railway was constructed by the province of New Brunswick under an agreement that the old Intercolonial would operate it. The Intercolonial took 60 per cent of the receipts and the province of New Brunswick 40 per cent, the latter guaranteeing the bonds and paying the interest thereon.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

I do not want to delay my hon. friend, but I really have only one object and that is to see that unprofitable lines are not built. Would my hon. friend say that before he gives his guarantees he will get a certificate from the Board of Railway Commissioners that it is in the public interest?
I certainly will not undertake anything of the kind. That would be placing the Canadian National system under a disability that no other railway suffers from.

The Canadian
Pacific is in that position to-day.
Not at all. The Canadian Pacific cannot locate its line, the Board of Railway Commissioners do that, but the company is not compelled to say whether the line is going to pay or not.

Will my hon.
friend say that the board cannot stop any Canadian Pacific construction that involves duplication?
I admitted that some time ago, but my hon. friend said the line must not be built unless we get a certificate from an outside body that it was going to pay.
In the public interest that is all I say.

Parliament must depend
upon the men who run the Canadian National railway and if we are going to take the advice of any person it must be their advice. I did not draw the act that excepts the Canadian National in the Board of Railway Commissioners in the matter of location, that was put through the House before my time and I am not responsible for it. It may be right and it may be wrong, that is not the question. The question is should this line be built. I was proceeding to point out to my hon. friend that although theoretically he had made out a case for running rights, yet when it came [DOT]down to practice, it would be impossible to get running rights at all over the lines which he suggests could be used for that purpose.
Then my hon. friend referred to the ratio on the St. John Valley railway which I was describing when he interrupted me. The ratio is high, and the ratio is high in the whole Atlantic region,-and I want to speak of that in a moment-but let me point this out: My hon. friend himself admitted that the proposition would improve the ratio of operating expenses against revenue, but he said it would only improve it a little. Well, the Canadian National railways are made up of a conglomeration of systems, and it is by these little savings and reductions of ratio all over the entire

system that the management is going to be able to bring it to a point where it will pay approximately. It will take many years, I admit that, before it will be able to pay its carrying charges; but if we are going to reject all these little savings because some person objects to them then we will never get the operating ratio down to a place where it will balance the revenue.

My hon. friend

If the amendment made by the committee was carried out and the line constructed for 115 miles from Bengough, it would carry the construction to a point in the seventh range, completely serving the people who really require this service very, very much. I am quite sure the people of the whole district want the line built where it will do the most good. I do not wish to take up time in a lengthy discussion of this bill. I submit that if the management be not forced to build from Radville in a southerly and westerly direction but be given the opportunity, after making a thorough survey, to build from either Radville, or Ritchie, or Bengough it would be the most satisfactory solution of this ques-

I presume the minister is going to enlighten the committee on the proceedings of the International Labour Conference.

The expenditure under this head

What was the expenditure last year?

The expenditure last
year was only $6,644.47, by reason of the fact that there was only one item on the agenda for discussion at the conference, that item being workmen's compensation, in which the provinces alone are interested. Therefore, only one federal government delegate was sent from Canada, and the Commissioner General at Paris acted as our other representative.
The Auditor General's report gives the expenditure at $12,645.83.
My hon. friend will recall that the Auditor General's report deals only with expenditures up to March 31, 1923. The expenditure for the last fiscal year is not yet before us.

Where a representative of or an adviser for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association or a representative of Labour attends these conferences the living allowance is $15 a day. Section 389 of the
Peace treaty provides that the representative of the employees shall be chosen from the organization chiefly representative of the work people, and it is claimed that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada answers this description in respect to the work people of Canada; therefore under the previous government and under this government the congress has been deemed without question to be entitled to name the representative.	.

As I stated a few
moments ago, the item on the agenda last year was workmen's compensation. So far as Canada is concerned, that is a matter in which the provinces are specially interested, the federal government having no authority to deal with it. The results from these conferences are slow at times in becoming manifest in the form of social justice for the workers of the world as contemplated by the Peace treaty. There have not been as many ratifications of conventions emanating from the International Labour Office as have been desired by the director and officers of the International Labour Conference, but very many nations have taken action to deal with some of .those conventions. These have been set out in detail from time to time in the Labour Gazette. The following brief summary may be of interest to my hon. friend: A considerable increase is noted during the past year in the number of ratifications by various countries of the draft conventions adopted by the International Labour Conference (League of Nations) at its annual meetings. The Secretary-General of the League of Nations has been advised of 93 ratifications of draft conventions by various countries. In addition to the 93 ratifications recorded by the I.eague of Nations, 58 other ratifications have been authorized by the competent authority in different countries but have not yet been formally communicated. My hon. friend from
Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) made some inquiries yesterday as to harvest excursions being run from the Maritime provinces, and I intimated that the Lhbour department had found some diffidence on the part of the governments in the Maritime provinces in respect to having harvest excursions run from those parts during the harvest season, to take farm labour out to the Canadian west. Last year we again had this matter before us, and on June 21, I wrote the following letter to the Prime Minister of New Brunswick, a copy of which was also sent to the Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, and the Prime Minister of Prince Edward Island:
Ottawa, June 21, 1923.
The Honourable Peter J. Veniot,
Prime Minister of New Brunswick,
Fredericton, N.B.
Dear Mr. Premier,
Crop reports from western Canada indicate at the present time the probability of an even larger yield of grain than the splendid results of last year's harvest, and it will be necessary within a very few weeks to give consideration to the matter of directing harvest workers from other parts of Canada to the prairie provinces for the harvest period. The need of the prairie province farmers for outside help will be for not less than thirty thousand and may even run to a considerably larger number.
As you are aware, it has been the practice of the railways to run excursions from the Maritime provinces, Quebec, and Ontario as far west as Sudbury, at very cheap rates for the purpose of assisting in the harvesting of the western crop. During the past three years very cheap rates have also been provided from the Pacific coast in order that all the available help in Canada might be pooled for the purpose of ensuring that the crop would be fully harvested.
The policy of running these excursions from certain sections of the Maritime provinces has not always met with the unanimous approval of all the interests affected, and there have on occasions been somewhat strong protests voiced against this policy. These protests, I think, have been based mainly on the ground that the excursions resulted in taking labour from the Maritime provinces to an extent which unduly depleted the provincial labour market.
As we shall in the very near future have to discuss with the railroads the subject of making adequate arrangements for providing the Prairie Provinces with labour sufficient to handle this year's crop, I should like to be advised as to your views with respect to the subject of the railways running excursions from your province, and I shall greatly appreciate your favour if you will write or wire me promptly stating the position of your government in this matter.
I feel sure that in determining your attitude upon this matter you will not fail to take into consideration the fact that the western crop is one of the fundamental and most valuable of our national assets and that the measure of our success or failure in the harvesting and handling of same reflects itself upon the general prosperity of Canada.
For your information I may say that I am forwarding an identical letter to the premiers of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
Yours very truly,
James Murdock,
Minister of Labour.
To which Premier Veniot replied under date of July 5.
My dear Minister,
I am in receipt of yours of the 21st of June re the policy of excursions from certain sections of the Maritime provinces to the West, in order to help in the saving of the harvest and I note that you would like to be advised as to my views with respect to this matter.
In reply I beg to say that I have discussed the matter with my colleagues in the Executive Council and we are of the opinion that while it is necessary that labour should be procured to help save the harvest in the West, we do not think that it is fair to have an excursion with rates fixed the way they have been in the past, when the people of our province were induced to go west at a very low rate of travel, but in order to return home, had to pay more than for the trip to the West. We feel that if the same rate going would be given for the return trip, that less of our people would be liable to remain permanently in the West, as in many cases we have discovered that some had difficulty in raising sufficient funds to return home, notwithstanding that they desired to do so. Otherwise I see no objection.
This letter is signed by the Premier of New Brunswick. On July 10, I replied to the premier indicating that we would do what we could to ensure the same rate of return, and intimating to him that outside of that objection we understood that he was not opposed to the running of excursions from New Brunswick. Last year they were run from no further east than from Moncton to the West.

However, I should like to impress this on him and I trust he will not forget it-that the Premier of New. Brunswick did not speak for the farmers of that province. There is no question about that, because our farmers in New Brunswick resent these excursions and have done so for years. We have never been able to get any satisfaction from anybody in regard to this matter; the correspondence read to-night is the first intimation that I have ever had that

anybody was ever consulted in New Brunswick. I should like to impress upon the minister just as strongly as I can the fact that it is very unfair to our farmers who hire their men by the summer for this special inducement to be held out to take the men to the West when they are so badly needed at home at that time of the year.
There was another point brought out by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and it was this: These men come back in winter and we are not in such a situation as they are in Ontario: We have plenty of work for them in winter; our men are not at a loss for work at any time in New Brunswick; in fact, our lumbermen are anxious to have them before we are through with the harvest. We have no idle men in New Brunswick. There is plenty of work for them all the year around, and there is no necessity for taking them away when we can provide them with work and certainly need all the men we have.
In New Brunswick we are up against another situation for which, of course, we cannot blame our own government, only in so far as it is a fact that conditions are not as good in our own country as in Maine. I live in what is known as the potato belt, which includes part of New Brunswick and part of the state of Maine which territory is separated by an imaginary boundary line. The Maine farmer is able to purchase his fertilizer anywhere from $8 to $10 a ton cheaper than we can in New Brunswick. That will be overcome by putting fertilizers on the free list this year however. But due to the fact that the Maine farmer can get 50 cents per hundred pounds more for his potatoes than we can-because we have to pay a fine of that amount in order to get into his market-he has been able to pay higher wages than the New Brunswick farmers can afford to pay. There is another drain on our help in addition to the inducement held out to our men to go west. These are serious handicaps, and the wages question is a serious problem for us because we cannot afford to pay the wages that the Maine farmer can although we are compelled to do so. I have had to pay $6 and $7 a day to young fellows to dig potatoes, but a man will go to extreme lengths to save a perishable crop before the bad weather sets in. The circumstances I have outlined show the position of the potato growers in my section of New Brunswick.

speechtext:
The second line of criticism on which I would like to say a final word is more acutely conceived. I have known it argued somewhat paradoxically that the Unemployment Insurance Scheme has been too successful, that it has been a mere palliative, that it has dulled the symptoms of unemployment and so made it possible to avoid a cure.
Let me admit at once that unemployment benefit has been a palliative, but a very necessary one. It is not too much to say that the provision of benefit has saved this country from an upheaval, the consequences of which might easily have been disastrous. Even as it is great numbers have suffered and are suffering severe privation and hardship. But it is probable that the total burden of distress and suffering has been lighter than it was in past years when unemployment was less pronounced and of far shorter duration.
When it is contended therefore, that the unemployment 'insurance scheme has prevented a remedy for unemployment from being found, I think rather less than justice is done to a valuable specific for this terrible disease of modern industrial organization. I am not going to attempt any answer to the question whether there is a remedy-that is a question of political therapeutics on which there is room for much discussion and for more than one opinion. One thing, however, is certain. The immediate cause of our great and long-continued unemployment is the failure of foreign trade. Until that revives, there is little likelihood that the industrial population of this country, organized and distributed as it now is, can again be restored to full employment.

The minister has
just given us some information in regard to the operation of the farmers' harvester exclusions. Now, last night I asked whether he had any influence in arranging for the rates which were given, and I believe he said, No. Yet, from the statement which he presented a few minutes ago he has been writing to the Premier of New Brunswick with a view to arranging this matter. I should assume from the minister's remarks that he has had something to do with these excursions. What I want to emphasize-and it is the very matter that the Premier of New Brunswick emphasizes-is the fact that it was the habit for a good many years to grant a very low rate to these people to go out to the West. When the work in the West was completed many of them had enough money to pay their fare back but had no means when they arrived here. The consequence is that by charging for return fare a rate almost double the fare to the West many of these people congregate in the large centres of Ontario and the local authorities have to maintain them during the winter. This is a very serious matter. We have had professional harvesters in this country who do nothing else but go out west during the harvest time to harvest. We have had them parading around Toronto and even coming down to Ottawa. Some men came from the Old Country to harvest the western crop last year and who apparently have done

nothing since the crop was harvested but reflect on the industrial conditions in this country. Because they have been very assiduous in scattering broadcast throughout the Old Country reports that there are thousands of men out of employment in Canada. We cannot get these men to do anything else but harvesting no matter what work you offer them, and I was glad to see the ringleader was sentenced to six months in gaol last week.

My hon. friend yesterday asked:
Does the minister exercise control over the rates?
My answer was "Not at all," and it may be possible I gave my hon. friend a wrong impression. As a matter of fact the Labour department does negotiate with the railways on two questions that affect the railway rates. One is the question of securing a continued rate for the removal of surplus unemployed labour from one province to another. Under the arrangement that we have had since I have been in the department, although it is made to run for a few months at a time usually and then is re-instituted as from the date of expiration, that rate is 2.70 cents per mile for the removal of surplus labour from one province to another, with a minimum of four dollars. In other words, the 2.70 cent rate would apply when the reduced rate ticket is four dollars or more. I realize fully that we are in a very favourable position to be criticized by the farmers of the Maritime provinces of Ontario as regards these harvest excursions, while on the other hand, our good friends from the western provinces want to get all the assistance that the Labour department can give them in times of stress to ensure a proper supply of labour to harvest the western grain crops. So, officers of the department do make certain representations to the passenger departments of the railways in regard to the rates both from the Pacific coast to the prairie provinces on certain occasions and from the Maritime provinces or Quebec or Ontario to the West. We do not exercise control. We only make representations for a rate that will meet the purpose desired, and offer encouragement to the young men to go to the West and help with the harvest. We do not want, of course, to deplete the farms of New Brunswick or Nova Scotia or Ontario or Quebec, but we are between two fires, 'as it were, and the department wants to be as helpful as possible in the matter.

think it fair that after these men are taken out to the West, they should be charged to come back nearly double the railway rates that they were charged going West, and realizing that there is no work for them when they come here, to land them stranded in these old provinces where they will have to be maintained by the cities? Does the minister think it fair that they should be charged these exorbitant rates coming back?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
In the great majority of
cases there is no such happening as that pictured by my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland). The average harvester last year was getting six dollans a day for harvesting and he did not need to work many days to earn enough to take him home. That sort of talk is absurd. I do not impute any absurdity to the hon. member's statement because I know he is talking candidly.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
How long does the
harvest last in the West or any other part?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
Six weeks, or probably two
months, sometimes longer. I have seen the harvest last for three months. I have paid as much as S350 to $400 to one man for harvesting and threshing. Two-thirds of the harvesters who come West come from Toronto, Montreal and other big cities. We do not get many men from the farms.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: Yes, you do.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: I cannot get them anyway. Two-thirds of these men would not be of any use to the farmers of Ontario. They come from the cities out West for the wages, and we have to board them for nine or ten days before they are of any use. We have to' feed them a little before they can do any work on the farms. All this story about not being able to get enough money to come back is just so much moonshine.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
The ra^e in 1922 from
Moncton to Winnipeg was twenty dollars, while the return rate from Winnipeg to St. John or Moncton was twenty-five dollars. I think that is about a fair comparison with what the rate usually is. I should like to ask the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) what he would think we should do when we receive a telegram sent on July 17 when the harvest is just commencing, and reading as follows:
Meeting this morning confidential statement will be prepared for press Manitoba requires fifteen Saskatchewan thirty-three and Alberta thirteen thousand harvesters three thousand available locally each province first excursion for Manitoba to arrive August seventh Saskatchewan and Alberta August fifteenth wages
probably three fifty for stooking and four dollars tu, threshing. Meeting later of railroad officials to consider points your wire fourteenth result to be announced later.
In other words, pressure was being brought to bear upon the Labour department and the Director of the Employment Service to do something. We could not, under those circumstances, decline to do what might be possible to assist the West, even though, by so doing and without personal knowledge, we may have helped to deplete somewhat labour in the Maritime provinces or Ontario or Quebec.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
I notice the minister
said that no excursions ran from Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. What was the tenor of the reply from the premier of those two provinces last year? Did they object and was that, why they did not run the excursions?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
The Premier of Nova
Scotia on July 17 wrote this letter:
Referring to your letter to me of the 21st ult., asking for an expression of opinion as to the advisability of advertising railway excursions from the Maritime provinces for harvesters, I beg to advise that as far as I was able, I consulted with my colleagues and others, and it was the consensus of opinion that it would not be desirable to make any special efforts to attract harvesters from Nova Scotia. This opinion would cover your desire to be advised as to my views upon railways running excursions from Nova Scotia.
We got a similar reply from Prince Edward Island.
# Mr. CHURCH: Some of the larger municipalities have grievances about the way in which they have been treated as regards these harvester excursions and the way those known as British harvesters were used. In my opinion, the British harvesters did not get a fair deal from the Labour department. They were brought out here by railway and transportation companies. They went out West, did their work, and when they came back to the large city of Toronto seeking work and finding none they came down to interview the government, but they were all sent back to Toronto. The city of Toronto wishes to protest against this to-night. It is a dumping ground after the harvest is over, for a large portion of the unskilled harvest labour that comes from the West. Dear knows, _we have, unfortunately, owing to many industrial troubles in that city, enough men of our own out of work without being made the dumping ground for the whole of Canada. As regards some of the men that came down to interview the government, it was said by some ministers that the men did not want to go to

Supply-Labour

work. To show that that is not the case, three of these men took jobs at snow cleaning at Mimico and three of them were killed there in the yards of the Canadian National Railways, where they were getting the mean wage of fifteen to twenty-five cents an hour shovelling snow. I protest against the way in which these British harvesters were used. I do not say that the government is altogether responsible for this because I think part of the fault belongs to the transportation companies; but I urge upon the government that if these men are brought out, they should not be brought out in September, October, November, December and January when there is practically no work, and people are out of employment. There should be a closed season for immigration in winter as in some of the larger municipalities we shall have to go back perhaps next winter to the dole system. The way these British harvesters were used was bad advertising for Canada in the Old Country. In connection with immigration agents, I do not say that the Minister of Labour is to blame for this particular case, because this may not come under his department, but in immigration matters and in bringing men to Canada there should be co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities on immigration matters in general. The cities and municipalities all have their own labour troubles to contend with and in winter, by reason of natural conditions arising in their own limits, they have enough unemployment to take care of without having men who are imported from outside dumped upon them and left to depend upon charity. Many of these men who are brought into this country from the Old Land and left to shift for themselves in our cities in winter have wives and children depending upon them, and some of them are men who have fought for the flag. This sort of thing gives this country a black eye and something should be done to remedy the situation. This matter may not come within the minister's department, but I would suggest that, this notwithstanding, he urge upon his colleagues to do something in the way of co-operation with the Old Country authorities, the transportation companies, the provincial governments and the municipalities, with a view of having some joint satisfactory arrangement arrived at to check this work up. The larger municipalities are^ protesting; as I say, they have men of their own to look after in the winter. The minister has made the statement that unemployment was not so bad; personally, I have never known it to be as bad as it was during

the last winter. Many of the industries are closed altogether and 50 per cent of them are running only 25 to 30 per cent of their time. The government, I submit, can exercise control, through the Railway Commission, over the transportation situation, and in my opinion the damage done to these men should be collected from these companies. These men have been brought out to this country under false pretences: they were told that there was plenty of work for them on the farms in the summer and that in the winter they could get jobs in the cities. The British Welcome League in Toronto had to be reformed to help these poor men, give them accommodation and house and feed them. I cannot over-emphasize the mistake that was made in bringing these people to Canada in the first instance; and if the government did not enter into any contract with them, then the least they should do is to find out who did, and bring the parties or companies to time. As a result of this misrepresentation these unfortunate men have been stranded in this country. I do not say that the Ministei of Labour is to blame; indeed, I believe he has done what he could himself to remedy things. I would suggest that during certain winter and semi-winter months there should be no immigration; there should be a sort of closed season for immigration. At all events, I think it is highly improper that men should be brought into this country in the depth of winter and then abandoned and left to shift for themselves with their families and ill fed children as a result of the misrepresentation of immigration agents and the greed of transportation companies. It was a bad advertisement for Canada in the Old Land the way our kith and kin, many of them returned soldiers, were used in this unfortunate British harvester episode.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
The government of this
country brings out a number of harvesters who are an asset to the West while the harvest is on. They are brought for that purpose and they render a certain service. They are well paid, of course, but I presume that those who pay them believe that they are getting value.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: No, sir.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
An hon. gentleman says
they do not get value. Why do the farmers employ these men, then? They are the best help that can be got, and are brought three thousand miles to be of service on hon. gentlemen's land. What I object to is that while these men are brought out to be an asset to the West, the moment they become

Supply-Labour
a liability they are dumped upon the cities of Winnipeg, Toronto, Hamilton and Montreal. I do not ask the farmers to keep them all the year, but I do say that the government that undertakes to bring men out in such large numbers for a specific purpose surely has some responsibility for their maintenance when their service has been rendered; at any rate, the government has a responsibility for providing for their return home. Why should the cities and towns have this liability imposed upon them such as they have had particularly in the past year and in previous years? It simply means that out of private charity hundreds and sometimes thousands of men have to be maintained throughout the winter period, and maintained by people who did not bring them out. and who could not possibly derive any benefit from them. The residents of the cities are under the necessity of maintaining these men if they do not wish to see them die on their doorsteps. I say that the government that brings them out ought to find means by which they can be employed, or at least fed, when their services are no longer required and they become a liability. If they are to be a liability on any one, it should be the government that brought them out and not the municipalities who should be responsible for them. Surely it is not beyond the genius of this government, which is made up of geniuses, to formulate some plan whereby this burden may be removed from the shoulders of innocent people, who cannot benefit in any way by the presence of the unemployed, and placed, if not on the shoulders of those who have benefited from their labour, at least upon the nation as a whole. Certainly, no individual section of the country should be made to bear the brunt of this condition. I think the Minister of Labour might signalize his term of office by creating a great reputation, if he would devise a plan by which these people could be properly taken care of and not left as a burden on people who have had no part in hringing them out. I suggest to the minister that he take the matter up in council and see if there is not wit enough there to do something to relieve the situation, and take care of these men when unemployment is unavoidable. In a country such as Canada, with its rigorous climate, there must be always a good deal of unemployment in the winter, and the municipalities and such centres as Hamilton, London, Guelph and these other places, all have their troubles and their burdens in the shape of unemployment every year. That burden comes naturally in the care for their own men who have been employed in these cities during the period
149i
*when outdoor work is possible. But there comes a time when for three or four or five months there is no outdoor work to be done: building operations cease, road work ceases and the many other forms of work that must be done in the open are closed down. I believe that every municipality is willing to take care of its natural liability in that regard, but I do think that any city or town has a perfect right to protest against being shouldered with the burden of caring for those who are not a part of its local liability. I hope the minister will think enough of my suggestion to take it up with the members of the government to see whether some plan cannot be worked out in co-operation with the provinces and perhaps with the municipalities. Certainly these people (must be taken care of and at the present time the burden is forced upon those who have no responsibility whatever in regard to them. The matter should not rest there, and I am satisfied that something could be done to solve the problem. These people are here as a result of national activities and they should be taken care of by the nation.

speechtext:
I did not make any money cutting wood except enough to buy my working clothes.
I went back to Sudbury and then to a place named Burwash east of Sudbury; stayed a month there, then I came back and paid fare to Winnipeg; arrived there about middle of September. I could not make anything. I worked for my board and lodging in a candy manufacturer's; worked for about three months.
I went to the immigration office and complained. They told me they could do nothing for me except a job on a farm for $5 a month. So I came out and asked to get on the relief in Winnipeg but could only get on two days. Then I went back to the immigration officers and they took me in; I stayed there probably about a month and a half.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: What season of the year was he offered the So a month job?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
About Christmas
time.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: Five dollars a month, and his board and lodgings?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
I suppose so.
Then a job came in for a 1.000 hands wanted for the bush in B.C. 1 heard these were to be used as strike breakers, so I asked at the immigration office from one of the permanent staff and he said there was no such thing as a strike in B.C.
Then 23 of us who were on the immigration relief signed up for B.C. We came to Wardner, B.C. and found a whole crowd of strikers waiting for us. They told us that the men were all out on strike and asked us not to go to work. Twenty-one of us never went to work but another and I talked it over and thought as the immigration office paid our fare out that we should go to work and pay this amoimt back, which we did. We worked a month in the bush $2.50 with board.
I left there and came down to Cranbrook and stayed in Cranbrook a few days. Then I met Gilbert and we decided to go to Trail and try and get work and on our way we got in this trouble. I had no money for two days. We went into this house to try and get something to eat and as we had no money we took the rifle and sold it to get something to eat. $8 we got for it. We sold it. in Grand Forks. We got there by walking and freight.
We stayed in Nelson one night. Gilbert was a member of the G.W.V.A. so got a ticket from them for the night for a hotel.	,
The judge makes this comment:
I am leaving the writing of this letter to go into the court room to sentence two lads-one from Halifax, Eng., and one from Glasgow, Scotland, for theft. They were enticed out here by the shipping agents of the Canadian railway companies. They paid about $100 to these shipping agents who get their rake-off and the rest goes into the coffers of the raihvaj' companies. These poor dupes who are being enticed out to Canada on false and misleading promises are victims of railway corporation cupidity. These lads were eking out a precarious living in the bush of Ontario and the farms of the prairies until they had to take refuge with scores of others in the emigration sheds at Winnipeg. Then they were shipped out to take the place of strikers in the timber areas of East Kootenay; they were told by the emigration authorities (so they have stated to me) that there was no strike.
Reduced to starvation conditions these lads lifted a rifle from a shed to sell to get food. They must go to prison for this crime. I will impose a short sentence but they have pleaded "Guilty" and I cannot avoid sentencing them.

The railway companies and steamboat companies are agitating for more and more population. Not a thought as to the class so long as they can get the passage money. Not a thought as to the future of these penniless lads so long as their fares are paid and go into the "Receipts" column.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that when one comes into close contact with these men and realizes the brave struggle that many of them have put up in order to try and gain a foothold in this country, many of them having done their piece of work when work was available and were afterwards driven from pillar to post, some of them not fitted for the kind of work for which they were brought over, we ought to consider very seriously our whole policy, and I for one think we should rigourously refrain from wholesale condemnation of men who come to a new country to find that there is not the machinery here for fitting them into what, to them, are novel conditions.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
I fancy this is rather a
storm in a teacup. One would think from the remarks made by the members from Toronto that the sacrifices are made entirely by the large cities. Let me say that many of our best settlers on the prairies and, I suppose, in other parts of the country as well, were young men that came out just in this way. In fact my mind now reverts to a young man who came out with no knowledge of driving a team in Canada-of course, horses are handled differently in the Old Country-and Canadians were amused at the way in which he would talk to his horses, which would go just where they pleased. I will not say in what part of this chamber that man sits now, but he sits here. I think I could go over the country and find hundreds and thousands of such men. At the present time the farmers in the prairie provinces are doing their share in looking after these immigrants. They regard such men in the right light, for they realize these newcomers are living under entirely different conditions to what they have been accustomed. Very often when given a team of horses they will let them run away. I remember a case last fall: A young man was given a team to help stook-thresh, as we call it; he let his horses stand alone a short distance from the engine; when he wanted to stop them he said "whoa" and they stopped, he called to them a second time with the same result, but the third time they did not stop, they went home of their own accord and smashed the wagon and rack. Such mishaps will occur again and again, but the farmers realize that these men are inexperienced and

Supply-Labour
with training will become useful; therefore they are making a sacrifice to train them, paying them sometimes three or four dollars a day which is often more than they are worth, confident that they will eventually become good Canadian settlers. The Englishman likes to be free; he resents being herded in the fall of the year and being told where he should go. Nobody dumps him on Toronto or any other city; he simply goes there of his own accord. I would remind hon. members from Toronto that much of the money which those men are helping to make on the prairie farms finds its way eventually to Toronto. Much of .what we pay for our farm implements, our textiles, and our mortgage interest, finds its way to Toronto. And I think if you look at the Auditor General's report you will observe that last year the federal government paid out to Toronto for unemployment $178,000. So I think the people of Toronto have no reason to make very much complaint. Let each one do his share by these men who come from the Mother Country, from conditions that are not very favourable, to a new country where they will make good if they are given a chance. But, I assure hon. members, the farmers of the prairie provinces are doing their share in dealing with these newcomers. As I said before, they are paying them good wages and training them at the same time, knowing they will become useful later on and good Canadian citizens. I think far too much has been made of this matter. If we all do our share I do not think any one will be badly hurt, and we will have so many more good Canadians.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
Why do not the
prairie farmers employ these men during the winter months if they are doing so much to assist them?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
To my knowledge many
of these men were able to work during the winter months, at low wages it is true, but in very good homes where they would have a chance to learn how to handle horses and to farm. I know near my own 'home two immigrants were given such an opportunity by a farmer, but both refused. Later on last winter the farmer was himself doing chores on his two farms because he could not get help at what he considered a reasonable rate.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
In the Hansard report of my remarks yesterday just before the committee rose at six o'clock when referring to a man who was sentenced to gaol for six months in Toronto I find I stated that
the magistrate termed him a rebel. The newspaper report was that the man himself admitted he was a rebel, but, as I pointed out, it was the magistrate who said he was a rebel. In regard to what the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg has said, I wish to point out that I did not without good reason make the statement that I made. I heard this man in Toronto about two weeks ago make the most reckless statements that I ever heard and I could not help being surprised that he had been permitted to say what he did. He admitted that he was the leader of this farmers' movement. He was advising these unemployed men what to do in case they made a contract to go on a farm.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: Did the hon. member say the farmers' movement?

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: They claimed they were farmers-harvesters' movement, I should have said.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: Immigrants' movement.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman does not need to sneer at the immigrants. No province in Canada has done so much to bring people out here and to see them comfortably established as Ontario has, and that is why I asked the minister last night how it was that these men were charged a great deal more for coming back from the West than they were charged to get out there. The excursion rate from Ontario is $15 going West and $25 coming back. Ontario has for many years had to do that work itself; there has not been that co-operation between the federal government and the province that there should have been and the result is that Ontario has provided all the machinery for bringing these people out here and seeing that they are satisfactorily located with employers who will give them a reasonable wage and good care. It is the natural desire of nine-tenths of those who come to this country to become owners of land and to build up homes for themselves, and they are obliged to go to Ontario and obtain the necessary experience, because diversified farming is carried on there to a greater extent, I believe, than in the newer districts of the West at any rate. Well, a few mouths after they become installed with the farmer in Ontario they read about these excursions to the West. They are able to get out there at a low rate and get big wages and the result is that in many instances they become dissatisfied. Although they have made a contract perhaps for eight months of the year, the Ontario farmer realizes that there is no use trying to keep a man who wants
Supply-Labour

to leave; it is better to pay him off and let him go. And when these men come back the farmers whom they left under these conditions at the beginning of the harvest season do not feel like taking them in for the winter, because if another opportunity presents itself they will leave again. The farmers of Ontario have been maligned by many of these men, and the.arrangement entered into b}' the Department of Labour through representations made to the railway companies are in no small measure responsible for this condition. If it is advisable to have excursion rates, then give the men the same rate back that they get going out. I am not saying anything about the West that my friends from that part of the country need take exception to; they know this is the case. They know that it is necessary for them at certain times of the year to have a great deal more labour than they require at other times, and so long as that is the case there will be this going backwards and forwards between Ontario and the West, and there will be many men accepting these excursion rates and going out to remain there, but it is unfair to Ontario that these inducements should be held out at the very time of year when the Ontario farmer needs help the most. As to this man who was sentenced in Toronto two weeks ago, I stood there and listened to the statements he was making to the men before him, and had I had the authority I would not have hesitated to have him deported within an hour. He is not the kind of man we want in this country; he belongs to that disturbing element which are doing their utmost to create friction between the labouring classes and their employees. Our country with its great undeveloped resources affords ample opportunity to every willing worker who can come here, and will afford that opportunity for many years. It is not necessary for anyone to go around the streets of our cities and towns complaining that he is unable to get employment. It is not the case; I know of many contracts that have been standing idle during the last two or three years for lack of people to do the work. This is the condition of affairs in Toronto, and along then comes the minister and makes arrangements with the railway companies regarding these excursions. I thought it was the Railway Board who had charge of the regulation of railway rates, but we find the minister inducing the help engaged by the farmers of Ontario for a term of months to leave those farmers at harvest time and go to the West. Then we have hundreds of thousands of dollars paid out in doles to carry these people through the winter and we find people sneering at the farmer fMr. Sutherland.!
and saying that he will not take these men in for a few months. Those who are out of employment in Ontario are largely those who have refused to accept work in Ontario or who have gone out to help our friends in the West as a result of the inducements which the minister has arranged or is to-day offering to them through the excursion rates on the railways.
