speechtext: My hon. friend flatters me if he suggests that I fixed the rate applicable to these harvesters' excursions. The Labour department found out from the passenger departments of the railways what the rates were to be, because the excursions are believed to be a benefit to all concerned, to the western farmers and to the men who possibly want to be moved.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
An independent investigation into this British harvester matter was held by Canon Vernon for the Church of England in the diocese of Toronto. These men were sent back to the city of Toronto by the government of Canada. I will tell my hon. friend from South Oxford that while there may be an occasional one or two of them a socialist or an agitator, the great body of these men are British bom, and anxious to work. Here is a picture that appeared in the Toronto Globe of a military funeral that was given to three British harvesters who met death while snow-shovelling for the National Railways in the Mimico freight yards. These three men, George Platt, Frederick Ward, and
S.	J. Harper, had been in every British war since the Crimean. They were all married men, and they leave families of two, three and four children. The transportation companies brought these harvesters to Canada, and there was misrepresentation. These men are not loafers. I have seen many of them myself, and they are the best possible type of immigrants we could get. These three good returned soldiers were killed while out working in a snow storm at Mimico, seven miles from Toronto, and here is what Rev. Canon Vernon said at their military funeral in the Church of the Ascension:
They knew the bitterness of criticism and misrepresentation and they have answered with their lives. Last Saturday they went forth to their work and laboured until the evening, and, in the Providence of God, that evening was the evening of their life on earth.
These men, killed on the railway tracks, were not given a pension by the Canadian National Railways, and their wives and small children were left destitute. The Standard Stock Exchange and other bodies got up a public subscription for them. These men, after seeking work in vain for days, were

Supply-Labour
given work at Mimieo on the Canadian National Railways at fifteen and twenty cents an hour, and one night an engine, backing down on the track, killed the three of them. The National Railways have not provided any pension or made any other provision for their widows and families, and I hope the Minister of Labour will see that justice is done to them. There was an inquiry, after the funeral of these three men, into the whole question of who brought these immigrants here, the conditions under which they came to Canada, went out west and were returned to Toronto and other urban centres of population in Ontario, and the inquiry showed that the men were brought out here under misrepresentation, that the transportation companies were to blame. Here is the Toronto Globe, an organ of the government, criticising the government's policy in this regard. They say that the government should not have allowed these transportation companies to bring these men out here, these men who had served in every British war since the Crimean war, and whose wives and families are now left to be taken care of by charitable institutions in Toronto. I am glad to say that a large number of these harvesters who came out from the Old Country have got work in Toronto, because we are a British-born city, and we are not going to see men who have fought for the Empire left to be dealt with by charitable bodies. It is a disgrace to the whole country the way these British harvesters were used, and as the Rev. Canon Vernon says, somebody is responsible for bringing them out. I tell you that it was the biggest black eye that was ever given to British immigration. I do not wish to criticise the government so much, because I think the transportation companies put something over on them. We have the president of one of the transportation companies in this country talking of the need for immigration, and this is the way the transportation companies use the British immigrants when they are brought to Canada. The Canadian National Railways paid these men fifteen, eighteen or twenty cents an hour for shovelling snow. These men went out in the depth of winter and worked under intolerable conditions seven miles from the city of Toronto, and were killed during one of the severest storms. There have been several sermons preached from pulpits about them. I know the Minister of Labour sometimes takes the pulpit himself. I do not think he is to blame for this particular case, but I urge him to take this matter up and sermonize Sir Henry Thornton and see if he cannot do something to get pensions for the widows of these three British-born soldiers who were killed while working on the National railways. I think the government should hold an inquiry into the bringing out of these British harvesters. I wish to protest against the way they were used.

I protest against any such arrangement as that What is the object of that special rate? maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext: I want to address myself particularly to the minister. I want to enlist his sympathy in the matter. I wish to present the matter from another point of view than what the leader of the Progressive party would probably put forward. The railway companies-and in this case the National Railways especially-should bring back the men to their homes at the same rate at which they took them to the West. They are being sent there to meet the needs of the middle West, they are taken from their own provinces, and the least that could be done in fairness to the sections from which they come is to return them at the same rate. Is it fair to deplete certain portions of the Dominion in rnxier to meet the needs of the West, and to grant special railway rates to assist in that depletion? I submit it is not? Surely the members of the Progressive party are not in favour of granting special inducements that will be in the interest of one section of the country more than in that of another. If they are not, how can they reconcile that position with the fact that an additional charge is made for returning the harvesters to their homes. I would submit this to the consideration of the minister so that he may, if he thinks fit, pass on to the proper quarter any views that appeal to him, more especially the view that if harvesters are brought from the East to meet the needs of the prairie provinces there should be no increase in the rates but rather a reduction in order to facilitate the return of these men to their homes.

maintopic: INDEX NUMBERS (WEIGHTED) OF COMPARATIVE REAL WAGES, MARCH-AUGUST, 1923
speechtext:
There has been considerable criticism of the railways for taking harvesters west at a lower rate than is charged them to return. I submit that the railways are entirely responsible for that course. They take the men from congested districts of the countiy to the West where they will have an opportunity to make a new start. Before they do this they advertise that the return rate will be higher than the rate to the West, so that if the men take in the excursion they do so with a full understanding of what the return faTe will be. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) has just stated that the British-born among the harvesters deserve better treatment than they receive. I wish to say that last year there were 12,000 harvesters and only about 800 of them were dissatisfied. I submit that was a very gratifying result- there was less than one in twelve that did not fit in with his new surroundings. About the time that some dissatisfied harvesters held up the Prince of Wales at Winnipeg, ten of them refused an offer of 15 a day in the dis-
trict where I live. They would not work under such conditions for $5 a day, and I know that at that time the crop was not half threshed up in Alberta. There is always a percentage of dissatisfied men who will not accept the treatment offered them and go to work. I cannot understand any strong, unmarried man being in want in the winter after having worked at the harvesting in the West. If any such person found himself stranded it was his own fault. Some of the married men, however, were deserving of some consideration. Three years ago the city of Regina maintained eight hundred men for the winter. Two years ago they advertised that they were not going to feed men, unless applicants were able to prove that their condition was not due to any fault of their own. As a consequence they had none to feed. As long as municipalities will assume the burden of feeding men without requiring them to prove that their condition is not due to any fault of their own they will continue to have applications from needy men for assistance.

speechtext: Can the minister state what the policy of employment agencies is in regard to transferring labour from one province to another in case of a labour dispute? the policy of the employment offices of Canada under those conditions to assist in transferring labour from one province to another. If representations are made, as they were made during recent months in British Columbia when the I.W.W. had a lumbermen's strike, or if representations are made to the employment offices of the prairie provinces that labour is wanted, the instructions are that the superintendent of employment offices must state the exact conditions in effect at the point where labour is required leaving the workmen then to act in accordance with their own judgment. maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS

speechtext:
Urges Federal Enactment to Prevent Interlocking of Interests
Seeks to Arouse Public Opinion
Wynndel Co-operative Head Claims Growers Being Given Over to Combine
To the Editor of The Daily News.
Sir,-This is an appeal through your valuable and much circulated paper (and others in sympathy with the fruit growers, that will copy it) to bring before the public the fundamental cause for the deplorable economic condition prevailing in our industry. And to pray for assistance from other commercial units, public bodies, boards of trades, and our provincials and Dominion governments to help us out of the entanglement with the two commercial combinations operating in our four western provinces, and known as the broker-wholesale combination, controlling the distribution of our fruit and vegetable products.
The true commercial condition that we are subjected to is this: That before we can use these fruit and vegetable wholesalers as our distributors, we must engage their brokers as our brokers, so that they legally can sell our products to themselves. And if we refuse to concede to their conditions they will get these requirements some where else, when a quantity of our products will have to go to waste.
A much similar condition prevails with the wheat and cereal farmers on the prairies, as their products must pass through the Winnipeg Grain exchange, a legalized gambling institution, for want of something more economic at present.
Farmers Discriminated Against
You men of commercial brain, as well as you lawmakers for our provinces and our Dominion, must realize the deplorable state of affairs that such a condition creates, for in no other industry would the laws permit such a condition to prevail, and if they did, no other industry subjected to it could ever hope of surviving beyond its stage of infancy.
Had nature not endowed the agricultural class with such a tenacity of life, it would, as an industrial unit in the nation's organic life, have been extinguished long ago.
We now appeal in the name of the British Columbia fruit industry to all fair-minded citizens to assist us in bringing to the attention of the governments in each of the western provinces and at Ottawa, the immorality of permitting interlocking combination in restriction of legitimate merchandising of the farmer's products, such as prevail with the mutual brokers, operating for the so-called Nash houses and the Growers Sales Agency, operating for the so-called independent houses.
[Mr. Murdock.J
As long as these two combinations are legally permitted to operate there is no hope for the British Columbia fruit industry ever getting out of the path
of bankruptcy, organized or unorganized. And the much hoped for co-operative movement of last spring only serves to hand the growers over to this combination in an organized form.
No Need to Buy Out
Mr. Howe of the Associated Growers says that it will take two and a half million dollars of the grower's money to get out of this broker-wholesale combination. Whereas we maintain that an order in council with the stroke of the pen, or the passing of an act by our federal government, would accomplish the same by making it unlawful for any wholesale house to own, control, or have any interest in any brokerage concern handling commodities of the same class as the respective wholesalers.
As farmers and fruit growers, we wish no quarrel with any legitimate wholesale house. On the contrary, we wish to foster a closer and more friendly relation along economic lines.
The wholesalers would not be human if they did not use to their own advantage the inquity of the law permitting such an interlocking combination to operate amongst us.
When we consider that the farming class constitute the Old Dad of the nation, providing the victuals for its inner sustenance, it becomes inconceivable that its family should subject him to bankruptcy, knowing, as they must, that it finally is bound to reflect upon themselves, causing suffering, if not social collapse.
On behalf of the British Columbia fruit and vegetable industry,
O.	J. WlGEN.
Wynndel, B.C., March 6, 1924.

one or two, such as the boot and shoe men and the plumbers?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
I have just read a
newspaper article, but I did not give the names of any persons or indicate in what part of the country they were located. I think as much or more information than that has appeared in the press from time to time.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Would the minister inform the committee if the Combines Investigation Act would meet the case complained of, providing the necessary charge were properly filed?

Supply-Labour

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Personally, I am of
opinion that a thorough investigation under the provisions of the act could be initiated if the charge were regularly laid; but it is a question whether the department should initiate such an investigation on the representations contained in this newspaper article. After we get further information from an officer of the department who is inquiring into the matter in Vancouver and elsewhere it may be considered that there is sufficient involved to warrant our asking council for the appointment of a commissioner to make an investigation.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Did the signer of that
letter refuse to file any formal complaint when invited to do so?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
He has not definitely
refused, but he has not yet laid a formal complaint.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
The reason I ask is that
the charge in the letter as published is of a very sweeping and a very damaging nature. I know nothing about it myself, whether it is even approximately correct or not. It does seem to me that an effort should be made, on the one hand, if the charge is well founded, to remedy the situation; on the other hand, if the charge is not well founded, to dispel from the public mind the idea that such a nefarious combination exists; and I think the minister should press for particulars of a definite character in connection with such a serious charge.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
I agree with my hon.
friend entirely, and I would not have felt it proper to place before the House references to certain concerns but for the fact that the letter had been published in the press. I would not think it proper to subject a business man to the notoriety of having his business methods condemned broadcast unless the charge was well founded. I believe, with my hon. friend, that after such investigation as the department may make it should indicate in some measure what are its views on the facts alleged in this communication.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
I am personally acquainted with the writer of the letter which the minister has just read. He is a thoroughly responsible and reliable man. For some time he has been head of a very flourishing co-operative association, and he is, I believe, in a position to give very valuable information regarding the conditions complained of. Although perhaps he may hesitate to file a declaration signed by six citizens, I think
that on the strength of the charges he has made it would be well for the department to institute an investigation under the act.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: We wrote the gentleman on March 20, but he has not even favoured us with an acknowledgment. We proceeded to make inquiries concerning the statements contained in the published article and are continuing those inquiries. We proceeded to make other investigations on the basis of the statements made in the published article, and are continuing those investigations.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: I take it that the department would eventually have some further progress to report, if investigations are still taking place.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: I hope so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Graham moves that item 277 be amended by adding thereto the following words after the word "registrar":
-which amount may be paid notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act or in the Combines Investigation Act.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: That is necessary in accordance with a letter from the Auditor General dated March 13.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Will the minister read the letter?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
It is as follows:
Dear Sir,
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 12th instant respecting a proposed remuneration to Mr. Hereford, a permanent employee in the Labour department, for his services as registrar under the Combines Investigation Act.
Any remuneration that may be proposed for Mr. Hereford will need to be voted notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act or in the act to provide for the Investigation of Combines, Monopolies, Trusts and Mergers.
Section 22 of the Civil Service Act prohibits payment to any permanent employee of the Civil Service additional to his salary unless specially voted by parliament and section 4, Subsection 2 of the Combines Act provides that in case the registrar holds office in conjunction with any other office in the public service he shall not be entitled to any additional remuneration.
The item in the estimates should, I think, provide as follows:
"Combines Investigation Act including $1,000 for the registrar, which amount may be paid notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act or in the Combines Investigation Act."
Yours sincerely,
Geo. Gonthier,
Auditor General.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
What other duties does
this gentleman perform, and what is his present salary in addition to the proposed $1,000?
Supply-Labour

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
For the past several
years he has been classified as an industrial engineer in the Department of Labour, and his salary for this fiscal year for that position is $3,615.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Are his duties as industrial engineer of a very important and onerous character? Do they occupy a large portion of his time?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Yes, he is busy all the time.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Some people can keep very busy doing nothing, but I will be charitable in this case and assume he has some duties. Could the minister tell us what they are?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: He is a technical officer who can deal with many of the questions that come before the department. His services are valuable also on account of the fact that the Minister of Labour has charge of the Printing Bureau. His work as industrial engineer and his recommendations in connection with the installation of machinery and the activities of the Printing Bureau have been extremely valuable and have resulted in a considerable saving to the government.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: How much of his time is now to be diverted from these highly important duties to the Combines Investigation Act?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
That depends on the
number of cases that arise. The department has not been extremely busy with cases arising out of this act, but there is considerable correspondence requiring attention and involving work which on many occasions has to be done after hours. It was thought that it would be well if we could get a responsible officer of the department to carry out these extra duties, and that it would be proper to give him additional compensation for that work.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: What was the total expenditure under this item last year?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Practically nothing-to
be exact, $82.24.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Would it not be possible to have this registrar's work done by some other official in the regular hours of employment without additional salary? The position is certainly a very modest one in spite of the rather distinguished title which he bears. "Registrar under the Combines Investigation Act" sounds imposing, I know, but the duties outlined by the minister do not seem to call for a very highly paid official. I am not

objecting to this form of paying the official, of adding $1,000 or of taking that amount out of this vote for the purpose. But in view of the situation disclc-sed during the past, year it does seem to me that one of the officers of the department could act as registrar without any additional salary. To add $1,000 to another salary of $3,600 for the purpose of administering an act that last year cost the country $82.24 seems to me to be carrying the thing a little too far.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: I should like to support that contention. This man has been relieved from certain duties that he had hitherto been performing, and I cannot see that there should be an additional salary. WTe are talking economy; why not begin along these lines?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
Very often my hon.
friend talks for justice, and I am quite sure that when he comes to analyse this question he will view it in that light. This officer is doing just as much work in his regular position as he was doing before, but it was not considered advisable that we should go outside and appoint some other person to this particular position. We want to economize; we want to carry on with as little expense as possible, and that we are doing so is shown in the expenditure of only $82.24 out of $30,000 voted last year.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: We want to prevent the minister from breaking his good record.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) suggests that we may not have much to do during the next year. That may be so, but we must be in a position to deal promptly and effectively with any cases that arise or any complaints that are made under the act. I do not think that even my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg or my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre would suggest that this is a situation that could be handled by any clerk in the department. It certainly deserves the attention of an employee possessed of more than ordinary capability and experience. That has been the thought at least, and I certainly hold that view. Now considering the actual weeks of investigation and research that have been entailed by these additional responsibilities thrown upon an officer classified by the Civil Service Commission as an industrial engineer, it does not seem to me unreasonable to ask that for the present fiscal year some additional compensation be given him. No additional compensation was paid from August last until March 31 of this year. The additional work and research was all undertaken free. I think it is only

Supply-Labour
reasonable to suppose that the registrar is better fitted to go ahead and determine what should be investigated during the present year by reason of this research work which he has already done, and I would hope that it will not be indicated here that we are not prepared to pay reasonably for extra responsibilities, service or duty required by a classified government employee.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
I think if we are to have
a registrar under the Combines Act, the House might very well vote the $1,000 that the minister asks for, but I would suggest to him that he might give this registrar some work to do, so that he can earn this extra salary. He might very well have him investigate, for instance, whether we have not a bankers' combine in this country that limits the rate of interest to depositors to 3 per cent. I do not think that he would have very much difficulty in proving that that is the case.
I would also suggest that the minister might have the registrar investigate and see whether we have not a millers' combine in this country. In support of my contention that we have a millers' combine let me just bring to the attention of the committee, that in Australia it is possible to buy a barrel of flour with the proceeds from four bushels and five pounds of wheat, whereas in Canada it takes the proceeds from six bushels and twenty-seven pounds of wheat to buy a barrel of flour I cannot understand why there should be that great difference in the spread between wheai and flour in Australia as compared with Canada. Flour is the basis of bread, which is the staff of life for all the people in this country, and I do not think it is right, when we have a registrar under the Combines Act, that he should allow this apparent combine to continue without making some investigation. In Alberta I believe you can buy flour that .is made in the city of Calgary for the same pricr in any part of the province, so there would seem to be some combine among the millers when they are able to fix a price for the whole province in that way. They also fix the price in Montreal at the same level as in Toronto, and sometimes they fix the price in Great Britain lower than it costs right here in Ottawa. I would suggest to the minister that he might very well have the officer in his department make some investigation into the millers' combine in this country.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
I must express my
surprise that so little of this amount that was voted a year ago has been used by the minister or the officers of his department. I have a very vivid recollection of how the minister
went up and down this country from one end to the other, railing against the trusts, mergers and combines that had everybody by the throat. We voted $30,000 a year ago, and the minister states to-night that of that amount it has not been necessary to expend more than $82.24 in order to settle this whole difficulty, and that now the coast is clear. I put some questions on the order paper during the session, and the answer with regard to this settlement that had been made was that it was not in the public interest to make known what had been done by this minister who has settled these combines once for all at a cost of $82.24 to the public. There is something so absolutely absurd about the whole thing that I am not at all surprised the minister should smile. We had evidence taken before a committee of this House a year ago with regard to the charges that were being made by the sugar refineries in this country. Sugar could be shipped over a long distance cheaper than it could be shipped to a point nearer to the refinery, and it was absolutely impossible for any grocers to buy except under those conditions. I brought this matter before parliament a year ago, but nothing was done. The minister, with all this $30,000 at his disposal, has not seen fit to take any action in that matter.
.The hon. member for Macleod has just referred to a millers' combine in this country. I think the millers of this country are being discriminated against to-day in the discriminatory freight rates that are being charged against certain points. Only last week my attention was called to the rates for flour and wheat from certain points, which showed that there is some discrimination being shown, and the result is that we have mills idle in many parts of the country to-day simply because they cannot compete with mills in other districts that are receiving a preferential rate. But the minister thinks all we have to do is to vote this money without being given any more information than he has seen fit to give to the committee, and he is even asking for $1,000 additional to be paid to some officer in his department. Surely the minister does not want the country to believe that these mergers, trusts and combines that were throttling industry and robbing the people of this country have all faded away since his advent to office, without any action on his part. If they have, I think it is up to him to inform the committee just what he has done in that regard, instead of answering a question I put on the order paper as it has been answered. My question was this:
1.	What prosecutions, if any, have been held under federal legislation against trusts, mergers, and combines
Supply-Labour

in restraint of trade in Canada during each of the years 1922, 1923 and 1924?
2.	What penalties were imposed during those years for the offences committed by any or all of said trusts, mergers and combines in restraint of trade?
That was answered on. March 20, as follows:
1.	During the year 1922 and until August 25, 1923, when a registrar was appointed under the Combines Investigation Act, 1923 the only federal legislation in effect under which prosecutions could be held was the Criminal Code (Sections 496, 497, 498). No prosecutions were held under this Statute. Under the Combines Investigation Act, 1923 no prosecutions have taken place, though complaints informally laid have been investigated with results which have avoided the necessity of prosecution.
2.	Answered by above.
I put another question on the order paper, with reference to the Combines Investigation Act, as follows:
1.	What complaints were laid and by whom?
2.	Against what persons, companies or corporations were such complaints laid ?
The anwer was:
It is not in the interest of the public to g:ve the information requested.
Does the minister want the members of this House to understand that if there are combines of that kind, and there are, the people should not know anything about them? Is it only the minister himself and those in the department who are entitled to know where these combines are located, and what means have been adopted in order to put an end to them? I do not think there is much evidence so far as the people generally are concerned that the minister has been active in this respect because, in so far as I can see, the very combine referred to by the member for Macleod (Mr Coote) is in operation. To-day we have vacant mills in the central part of Ontario that cannot be disposed of by reason of the discrimination that is shown in regard to rates. We have the sugar combine to which I referred which compels the grocer to pay those excessive rates. That grocer cannot have sugar shipped to him without purchasing from the wholesale grocers at a point distant from his place of business. He cannot purchase by the carload lot and have it shipped to him direct; he must go to the wholesale grocer at a greater distance. These are some things that the people are aware of. The minister ought to be frank and let us know in what respect he has relieved the people from the pressure that 'has been exercised by these combines.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
My hon. friend I am
sure knows what is largely, or most often, the cause of combines, I hope this government is going somewhat in the direction of removing the cause and that it will move further in that

direction. My judgment is that protection which has been improperly in effect in Canada has permitted some of the combines to grow, and exist and flourish; and if we can remove from Canadian business improper protection that only contemplates the protection of certain special favoured individuals we will remove combines that affect the welfare of producers and consumers largely from the realm of possibility. That is my opinion.
Now as regards my hon. friend's suggestion. I understood from the questions he placed on the order paper, and I understand now, that he would like me to give the name, and date and place of all the investigations, or inquiries, that have been made. Well, the two Houses of Parliament indicated that possibly that would not be the proper thing to do. The law itself contemplates that shall not be done unless real cause and necessity for it is shown. While those instructions are in effect I do not think it would be fair for me to say that we investigated Mr. Jones at such a place because it was alleged that he was conducting, or alleged to be conducting a combine in the plumbing trade, or Mr. Somebody else at another place because he was conducting, or alleged to be conducting, a combine in the boot and shoe industry. It would not be fair to do that and I think the discussion last year in both Houses indicated this view. I can assure my hon. friend that if he and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr Coote)-knowing all these facts as to the millers' combine that they have talked about-will touch the pen, and get sufficient other citizens of Canada to do the same, we will initiate an investigation under the Combines Investigation Act, and I personally will endeavour to see that we go to the full limit by investigation to secure all the facts possible; but until someone makes the application contemplated by the law I shall have to abide by the instructions of both Houses of Parliament as understood and not appear to harass business unduly, but act only as the result of securing complaint as the law requires over the signature of six citizens. Now, whether that is right or wrong it is the position that I contend the minister in charge of the department should take in view of the instructions of both Houses when this law was passed.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext:
It is rather difficult to allow to go unchallenged the little political byplay that the minister indulged in in the early part of his remarks He says that the government have gone in the right direction towards removing the cause of combines in this country by dealing with this iniquitous thing

Supply-Labour
known as protection. Will the minister say that the reduction of the duty on farm implements, for instance, is proof that there was a combine in restraint of trade-an unreasonable combine such as he referred to before his election to this House, and such as is contemplated in this act? Will he say such a combine existed up to the time this budget came down, and that the budget by the reduction of these duties dealt with that iniquitous combine?

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: I am not saying so.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: I am putting a logical interpretation upon the minister's argument. If the minister does not say that, if he cannot claim that, then his argument a moment ago is senseless, meaningless, and pointless.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Just a moment-

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Will the minister recall for a moment those vociferous denunciations of that terrible cotton combine-

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Textiles.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Yes, of the Canadian Cottons and Dominion Textiles, a combine that was grinding the very faces of the poor in the mud according to the minister's statements, in one of his numerous speeches before the election. He said the government has removed all these things because the other day he told the country that there is no combine in Canada. He said if you searched the country from the east to the west, from Halifax to Vancouver, there was no combine in Canada.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Neither the minister nor any officer of his department made any such statement. I want to challenge that now because my hon. friend and others have used that too often; you cannot get away with it. There are combines in Canada detrimental to the public interest and they should be dealt with.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: The minister now comes forward and makes these statements. He is Minister of Labour, administering the Combines Investigation Act on which last year he spent $82.24, out of $30,000 that parliament gave him for the purpose, and he declares to-night that there are combines in Canada that ought to be dealt with. Well, why does he not deal with them? Has he not the power under the Combines Investigation Act? He spent an hour a little while ago-

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: BAR WHOLESALE BROKER COMBINE WIGEN DEMANDS
speechtext: It seemed to me that he spoke almost for an hour. However, previous to a few moments ago he indulged for about

an hour-I think I have got it straight now- in a long dissertation, assuring the committee that after careful inquiry no combine was found; that a certain individual wrote him a letter, and that he looked into it and challenged the individual who made the complaint. Now he turns to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) and says "Put your finger to pen, and get six others to put their fingers to pen. and look out for what I will do." If the minister himself knows of combines why does he not himself put a finger to pen? Has he not sufficient power? Can the minister not get six of his friends to put their fingers to pen and make a charge against these combines that he knows to exist, that ought to be suppressed, that ought to be dealt with? The minister comes before parliament as a minister of the Crown and deliberately charges that he knows of combines that exist, that ought to be suppressed. Where are they? We have a right to know. That surely is not a secret sacred in the mind of my hon. friend. Has parliament no right to know where combines exist, where the minister knows that fact and how they ought, in the interest of public safety and having regard to public welfare, to be suppressed? Is parliament not entitled to know that? The minister has indulged in heroics in this chamber to-night. He indulged in heroics in a speech which, perhaps I have exaggerated a little. I admit that, but sometimes we have to exaggerate in order to stir the minister up, as I have succeeded in doing

I am going to repeat
it in a minute.

I would be surprised if
he did not repeat it in spite of his denunciations to-night.
I will give day and date and include some of my hon. friend's friends in it.

But if the minister is
going to make charges on the floor of this House and say in one breath that there are no combines, that they vanished simply because he got his act passed-that is one of the statements that he made to the public-
Not at all. I must tell the hon. gentleman that he is making a gross misstatement. I said no such thing. I shall be glad if the hon. gentleman will simply stick to the facts.
I have learned from experience that it is very difficult to put any interpretation upon the minister's remarks, because he invariably denies or twists his way out of them. Amy one who has read any
Supply-Labour

of his speeches or who has followed, in the slightest measure, in the most casual way, his speeches, knows perfectly well that he has time and time again charged that there are combines in Canada. He charges that tonight, and yet, although he pleaded with the people to let him once get info office and what he would not do with those combines was not worth talking about, in spite of two and one-half years in office, he has not discovered any. In all his reports to-night of incident after incident he, with a good deal of heroics and self-complacency, boasted that these persons who had charged or indicated that combines existed had failed to make good their charges. Now he comes before parliament and what we are dealing with particularly is the voting to an official who is already getting $3,600, or $1,000 additional salary, for the purpose of administering an act the expenditure of which last year was $82.24. In my estimation, the official who administered this act last year, who has been receiving $3,600, if he is administering this act, is not performing the duties that he was performing previously. I think that is a fair deduction to make. He certainly is not down in the Printing Bureau shifting printing machinery around and reorganizing the Printing Bureau; he is not advising the minister on that work-what was it the minister said?-he is reading and studying the records of other investigations and so on in order to fit himself for this job. A little less of these heroics, a little more common sense, a little more of performance and fewer charges would be more becoming to the minister.

Prom which source? I said and I repeat that, in my judgment, there are in Canada combines which should be investigated. I am substantiated in that view to-night by two hon. gentlemen who named them in this House. I think there may be others. I said something about combines and monopolies in the textile trade a few years ago. I think that could have been proven and I think it could be proven yet. A committee of this House, if my hon. friend will recall, with a member of this government sitting as chairman, investigated certain textile and other industries and found a percentage of profit brought about directly as a result of protection, that was absurd and unfair to the people of Canada. In 1920, when an investigation into the textile trade was instituted by a questionnaire sent out to all concerns manufacturing textiles in Canada, what was the result? At once the textile branch of the Canadian Manufacturers'

Association came to their friends in Ottawa and appealed to them, the cabinet with which my hon. friend was connected, to relieve them from being required to fill out that questionnaire. With what result? On the 27th January, 1920, they got a draft recommendation to council prepared relieving them from filling out those questionnaires, and on the 28th January the cabinet with which the hon. member was connected were challenged as to their right to relieve the textile manufacturers from filling out this questionnaire. With what result? They told the textile manufacturers that they should comply with the order of the board and fill out the questionnaire. When the questionnaires were turned in, what was the result? Profits of two, three, yes, and more than three hundred per cent were shown on the business of some of these textile manufacturers that you have been hearing tales of woe about from my hon. friends across the aisle during the past two or three years. Those profits were shown over their own signatures in a sworn statement, and my hon. friend's friends took care to see that, even though that was khown, there would be no interference with the business that they were conducting; that no action would be taken to prevent a recurrence of that, because they just proceeded' to make moribund, to put out of business, a board which was supposed to investigate and to deal under the law with those things to which I have referred. If my hon. friend wants information and data, why does he not insist on an investigation? These facts are not too old and too cold, and the data is not too much out of date to be looked into thoroughly in order that it may be found out whether the protection of the textile manufacturers was not simply taking unfair and indecent profits from the people of Canada for several years. Yet listen to the tale of woe that we heard last year about some of these concerns being put out of business, and that we have heard even during the present year. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre should realize that there is a long story to this, and I am personally willing to go into the whole story. But again I say to my hon. friend that even though holding the opinion that there are still in Canada combines that should be investigated, I know that parliament indicated last year the view that investigations should be initiated by six citizens of the age of twenty-one years. The view was, as I understand it, that there was to be no undue investigation or possibly undue interference that might develop later as being unfair to

Supply-Labour
some concerns. We are trying to follow that policy or what we regard as the instructions of parliament. Personally, I think it should be changed. I think an investigation might be very properly instituted on the signed statement of one citizen of Canada.

My hon. friend is
a member of the government and the government has control. I would ask him, what did he do in regard to Sir Charles Gordon whom he threatened to have gaoled when he was railing against trusts and mergers?

My hon. friend once
again is inaccurate; I have never in any speech in my life referred personally to Sir Charles Gordon. I d'o not think my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) will think it improper for me to call his aiten-tion to his own statement last year:
Why there would be no difficulty at any time, anywhere, day or night, summer or winter, to get six citizens of Canada to complain against some institution. I do not say ignorant people, but uninformed people are very prone to complain of businesses or institutions wherever they may be. Six uninformed, irresponsible individuals may ask for an investigation. The registrar proceeds to investigate. He calls for all documents, contracts, books and so forth of the company. He can step into the office, examine into prices, obtain any information he demands. All that he asks for must be produced; the concern which is the subject of inquiry has no recourse but to give up everything that is demanded pertaining to the secrets of its business. I submit that one rival desiring to get information regarding another rival's business, perhaps more successful than his own, perhaps underselling him on the market, would find it the simplest thing in the world to get that information through such an institution as this.
It. is that and similar representations made by hon. members of this House that lead me to the belief that we should go very carefully, and know our ground thoroughly, before undertaking an investigation that might later prove altogether unwarranted,. That is the reason, and the only reason, why some of the institutions which I think should be further investigated have not been inquired into and will not be inquired into, so far as I am concerned, under existing instructions and conditions and with the law as I see it.

My hon. friend undoubtedly has in mind the Board of Commerce Commission of which he was a very proud member when he refers to this application of the textiles for relief from answering a certain questionnaire. The committee ought to observe; in justice to the government which the minister condemns so vigorously, that no such relief was given to the textiles;
150i
and the minister of course is taking a great deal of credit to himself for that. Now, this whole quarrel, if I might refer to the matter in that way, between my hon. friend, other members of the Board of Commerce, and the preceding government, regarding the Board of Commerce and the acts controlling it, is an old quarrel Which the minister very frequently resorts to when he wants to escape an awkward dilemma. He tells the House that he personally as a member of the Board of Commerce was convinced, and so convinced that he vigorously protested against the government of the day taking action, that certain combines existed during the year
1920,	which was the last year of the preceding government, which was defeated in
1921.	The minister personally knows all that; yet he has been in office two and a half years and has not given the slightest indication, either before the passing of this act or since, that it ever has been his intention to make any investigation. He said to the House to-night, however, that this government had1 discovered a way to cure the very source of these evils, the means being to reduce and remove the protection on these various industries. Well, I do not think that the House has noticed very many reductions in the duties on cottons and textiles; there has been absolutely no indication of such reductions. I am not asking the government to make any reductions, but I do ask both the government and the minister to be consistent in their arguments. The minister condemns his opponents because they did not remove the protection on these industries, under which these combines grew up; but although he has been over two and a half years in office he and his colleagues have made no attempt to apply that remedy. Why? Largely because they are convinced that there is absolutely nothing in the minister's argument; there is no other explanation for it. I venture to say that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will scarcely corroborate what the Minister of Labour has said to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not corroborate what the hon. gentleman is saying now.
Will he corroborate the statement of his colleague?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not going to corroborate the statement of the hon. member that there was no reduction on textiles. There was a reduction under the British preference.

Yes, of 2i per cent.
Supply-Labour
Which we are told was enough to put half of them out of business.

Let me ask the minister,
has he fully dealt with t'he combines?
No, by no means.

Then we may expect
action from the minister in the future.
I hope you will get it.

Let me say in regard to
the quotation from my speech, which the minister has read to the committee, that I take exactly the same position now as I did *then, absolutely. I say that no investigation should rest upon the basis of a single complaint, as was originally intended in the act before it was amended in accordance with the present provision. I am satisfied that with the signed statement of six or more responsible citizens an investigation, under the act as amended, is warrantable.

And do you not think
that such is the plan which the department should follow?
In so far as the public is concerned, yes. But I do not think that the minister can shield himself behind that provision so far as he himself is concerned.
Is the minister's opinion worth more than that of any other citizen?

His opinion as the opinion of the Minister of Labour should be worth more than that of a private citizen, yes. The Minister of Labour has all the information to hand; he has all the facilities available to secure that information; and his opinion ought certainly to be worth more than that of a private citizen who has no such means of getting at the facts.

Is the minister aware that
last year a special parliamentary committee on Agriculture investigated ocean freight rates, and on April 23, 1923, they brought in their fourth interim report, which reads as follows:
Your committee are of the opinion that upon the regular steamship lines trading from Canadian ports the price of transportation service is determined neither by the law of supply and demand nor on the basis of cost plus a reasonable profit, but that a combine exists among the various shipping companies, which combine is known as the North Atlantic and U. K. Conference Eastward -bound.
As this committee was composed of nineteen members of this House, their number should at least be sufficient to demonstrate to the minister that a combine does exist. Under the circumstances I wonder if the government intends to do anything.
That particular question would come under another act. As a matter of fact I think it is being investigated1 at the present time.

By whom
is the investigation being carried on?
By persons who are qualified to investigate. I do not .think it would be advisable for me to say who are engaged in the work.

What department of the
government has the work in charge?

That would be more
closely connected with the Department of Trade and Commerce.
It would be true to say that the government has this matter under consideration at all events?

I think it is absolutely
correct to say so.

And that an investigation is
taking place?
I understand so.

How long
are these investigations to continue before the public may expect some action to be taken?

Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member's
question is not in order under this particular vote, the minister having stated that the matter referred to is under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
We are discussing combines.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
question was not directed to combines.

I wonder
how long the minister will consider the nature of these combines before taking action against them. Complaints have been registered in the press and by members on this side and a number of investigations have been held, yet we find the cattle and other freight rates still rising.

Mr. Chairman, I might advise the committee that the discrimination existing against Canadian products by the North Atlantic Conference has been corrected in part. We are following up other cases of discrimination.

Probably this will answer
my hon. friend's question. Is the British Imperial Shipping Committee, presided over by Sir Halford Mackinder, which was recentlv in Canada, dealing with this discrimination?

No; but as the result of our
representations they are looking into certain complaints.
That is in connection with the North Atlantic shipping rates?
Yes.

I understand that a committee investigated a shipping combine on the Great Lakes last season, and that the charges were substantiated. Is it the intention of the government to prosecute the offenders?
I cannot advise my hon. friend just what the government intend to do further in that matter.

Will the minister tell us
just how far-reaching the Combines Act is? Does it simply cover industries and not ocean freight rates?
It does not reach anywhere.

No, it would not have
anything to do with freight rates.
With ocean freight rates?

No, it would have nothing to do with ocean freight rates. The interpretation clause of the Combines Act reads as follows:
The expression "combine" in this act shall be deemed to have reference to such combines immediately hereinafter defined as have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others; and^ limited as aforesaid, the expression as used in this act shall be deemed to include (1) mergers, trusts and monopolies so-called-	,
(3) any actual or tacit contract, agreement, arrangement, or combination which has or is designed to have the effect of (i) limiting facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing; or (ii) preventing, limiting or lessening manufacture or production; or (iii) fixing a common price or a resale price, or a common rental, or a common cost of storage or transportation.
It has not even been assumed! by the Labour department that the Combines Investigation Act would cover an investigation of ocean or lake steamship rates.
A few minutes ago the minister stated that some of the textile companies were making enormous profits.
I know the hon. gentleman does not intend to misquote me. I said .that in 1920 the questionnaires filled out by the textile company indicated that they had made profits higher than 300 per cent.

That is, you did not
refer to the same companies as to-day making enormous profits?

There is a very great difference between the profits the textile companies were making in 1919-20 and the profits they are making to-day. Many hon. members tell us that the textile companies to-day have been put out of business by the 2J British preference of last year.
Does not the minister consider a combine on the Great Lakes as detrimental to the public interest as any combine that could be imagined?
I would say yes, probably a good deal more so.
Why should not they be included in the Combines Act?
They have been held to come under the Trade and Commerce department. As a matter of fact, an investigation was held under the direction of that department and a report made.
The minister has informed the committee that the protection enjoyed by those trusts, mergers and combines is responsible for the whole trouble we have here.

The minister did not say any such thing-certainly not in that way.
Supply-Labour
The minister attributed the existence of trusts, mergers and combines to the protection which they are to-day enjoying.
Largely as the result of unfair protection.

In the debate on the Address and in the debate on the budget the tariff was discussed, and now the Minister of Labour has interjected it into his estimates as well. It reminds me somewhat of certain gentlemen down in the Maritime provinces, who shortly after the Liberal government came into power in 1896 referred to the promises which they had made and to their unfulfilment in these words:
We promised them freedom from tariffs,
We promised them freedom from toil,
We promised to break up the robber combines for the tiller of the soil;
We have helped our friends wherever we could,
And we have made it rough for our foes,
But we have saddled the same old robber combines on our Lady of the Snows.
I think this very clearly shows how active the minister has been. He claims that while a member of the Board of Commerce he obtained an intimate knowledge of conditions prevailing at that time. It is rather remarkable that when put in a position of power and authority he has done absolutely nothing to check combines, mergers and trusts. Of the $30,000 that was voted a year ago he has spent only $82.24, and he comes back to-day and asks this House to vote him another $20,000 without giving us any assurance that anything is going to be done to these combines. "No," he said; "the remedy depends on reducing the tariff or removing it entirely." That is really the only remedy he has for ridding the country of the trusts, mergers and combines which have saddled themselves upon us during the last few years. It has been pointed out to him that he has referred to certain research work carried on by his department. Surely if his department has all this intimate knowledge as to these leeches which are sucking the lifeblood from Canadian industry, he is in a position to cure the evil. Surely it is not necessary for him to sit back in his seat and say: "Why, the requisite -application over the signatures of six citizens has not come to the department asking for such an investigation." That was not the intention of the act. With the officers of his department it is his duty to investigate, and the research work to which he has been referring ought alone to have placed at his disposal the necessary information-and he has told the committee that he has the inform-fMr. Murdock.]
ation-therefore I think he has been recreant in his duty as minister in not taking steps to put a stop to this condition of affairs. Conditions are not the best in this country, and if the condition exists that the minister acknowledges, then it is the duty of the government to see that the people are afforded relief from it.

There is no doubt about
this matter of a combine ion the 'Great Lakes, and I think the minister should give us some assurance that something will be done. I am satisfied, and I think others are too, that this condition still exists on the Great Lakes Perhaps they are not quite as bold as they were before the investigation, but I suppose when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) comes before us with his estimates he will say that it was a matter for the attention of the Department of Labour. I think we should have some definite statement in this regard.

That combine on the
Great Lakes was regarded as sufficiently important to call for the appointment of -a special royal commission to investigate and report.
Was that commission not appointed before we had the Combines Investigation Act?
Yes. I think the report of the commission was in before last August.

To what extent did the
government carry out the recommendations of the commission?

My bon. friend will
have to ask some other member of the government for that information. I suggest that he make inquiry of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he comes on with his estimates. The matter was under his direction.
